sounds.name: First Note
sounds.ref: Classic technique: the smallest Easel patch that plays from the keys
sounds.blurb: The complex oscillator, played from the keys, opened and closed by the envelope through Gate 1.
sounds.how: On the Easel the envelope is not wired to anything: its output is the orange jacks, and you choose where it goes. One cord from an orange jack into LEVEL 1 makes Gate 1 open with each touch and close again, and with the gate in combination mode the note gets darker as it fades, like a struck string. The oscillator plays the keyboard because its KEYBOARD switch is on.

steps.title: Envelope into Gate 1
steps.why:
Patch an orange envelope jack into the black LEVEL 1 jack, and raise LEVEL 1’s processing slider so the envelope gets through.
- Cord: envelope 3 → LEVEL 1.
- Gate 1 LEVEL processing 10, LEVEL offset 0: the gate is shut until the envelope opens it.
- Envelope trigger source keyboard, mode sustained: it rises when you touch a key and holds while you hold it.
- Listen for: a note on each key that stops when you let go, with a soft tail.

steps.title: A rounder tone
steps.why:
The waveshape knob mixes the sine with the square chosen on the switch below it; TIMBRE adds a little edge.
- waveshape 4: mostly sine, some square.
- TIMBRE 2.
- Listen for: a woody, slightly reedy tone instead of a buzz.

steps.title: Combination mode and a little reverb
steps.why:
Gate 1 in combination mode both opens a filter and raises the volume, so as the envelope falls the note darkens and fades together.
- Gate 1 mode select: combination.
- REVERBERATION 3.
- Listen for: each note dulling as it dies, with a short spring tail.

context.lpg1.levelCv: In this sound: how far the envelope opens Gate 1. Lower it and the notes get quieter and duller.
context.lpg1.level: In this sound: kept at 0 so the gate shuts between notes. Raise it and a quiet tone drones under everything.
context.env.decay: In this sound: the tail after you let go. Lower on the slider is longer.
context.cosc.shape: In this sound: left for a pure sine, right for more of the square.

tweaks.try: Switch Gate 1 to voltage cntrld amp
tweaks.hear: The notes keep their brightness to the end: only the volume falls.

tweaks.try: Pull the attack slider down to 4
tweaks.hear: Each note swells in over about a second.

sounds.name: Lowpass Gate Bongo
sounds.ref: Classic technique: the West Coast “bongo” pluck
sounds.blurb: A very short envelope strikes Gate 1 in combination mode: a hollow, woody pluck.
sounds.how: The lowpass gate is slow to close, so even a two-millisecond envelope leaves a note that rings and dies naturally, brightest at the start. That is the sound of a struck object, and it is the Easel’s signature. A little TIMBRE on a sine gives the hollow, bongo-like body.

steps.title: A sine with a little folding
steps.why:
Turn the waveshape knob fully left for the sine alone, and add some TIMBRE so the sine folds into a rounder, hollow tone.
- waveshape 0.
- TIMBRE 3.

steps.title: A strike, not a note
steps.why:
Envelope into LEVEL 1, set to transient with every time at the fast end: the gate gets a short kick on each touch, however long you hold the key.
- Cord: envelope 3 → LEVEL 1, processing 10.
- Envelope mode transient; attack 10, sustain 9, decay 8.
- Gate 1 combination.
- Listen for: a short, round pluck with a natural ring.

steps.title: A touch of room
steps.why:
Some spring reverberation puts the plucks in a space.
- REVERBERATION 3.

context.cosc.timbre: In this sound: the body of the drum. Up for a brighter, more metallic knock; down for a soft thud.
context.env.decay: In this sound: the length of the strike. Lower on the slider gives a longer, more marimba-like note.
context.lpg1.mode: In this sound: combination, so each pluck dulls as it fades. On lo pass filter the plucks have no front edge.

tweaks.hear: The pluck turns metallic, like a struck pipe.

tweaks.try: Set Gate 1 to voltage cntrld amp
tweaks.hear: A click rather than a pluck: without the filter there is no ring.

sounds.name: Timbre Surge
sounds.ref: From the Easel manual — Patch-chart 10, envelope on timbre
sounds.blurb: The envelope opens the gate and adds harmonics at the same time, so each note starts with a burst of brightness.
sounds.how: One orange output feeds Gate 1’s LEVEL and another feeds TIMBRE (the Easel’s banana plugs stack, so one envelope can go to two places). As the envelope rises the sine folds over and buzzes; as it falls the tone goes back to a plain sine while the gate closes. Brightness here comes from adding harmonics, not from opening a filter.

steps.title: A sine through Gate 1
steps.why:
Envelope into LEVEL 1, sustained, with a quick attack and medium decay.
- Cord: envelope 3 → LEVEL 1, processing 10.
- waveshape 0 (sine), TIMBRE 0.
- Listen for: a plain, flute-like sine.

steps.title: The same envelope on TIMBRE
steps.why:
A second orange jack into the black TIMBRE jack, with TIMBRE processing at 7.
- Cord: envelope 2 → TIMBRE.
- TIMBRE processing 7.
- Listen for: each note starting bright and buzzy and melting back to a sine.

steps.title: A slower decay
steps.why:
Pull the decay slider down so the tone takes its time to soften.
- decay 3.5.
- REVERBERATION 3.

context.cosc.timbreCv: In this sound: how bright the start of each note is. At 10 it snarls; at 3 it only colours the sine.
context.cosc.timbre: In this sound: the brightness that is left once the envelope has gone. 0 leaves a pure sine.
context.env.attack: In this sound: how quickly the brightness arrives. Lower for a swelling “wah”.

tweaks.hear: A harsh, brassy attack on every note.

tweaks.try: Set the waveshape switch to triangle and the knob to 10
tweaks.hear: The triangle folds too, with a hollower edge than the sine.

sounds.name: Pulser and Sequencer
sounds.ref: Classic technique: the Easel playing itself
sounds.blurb: The self-running pulser steps a five-stage sequence on the complex oscillator’s pitch and strikes the gate on every step.
sounds.how: The pulser, set to self, is the clock. Each time its ramp ends it moves the sequencer on a stage and fires the envelope, which strikes Gate 1. A blue sequencer jack goes into PITCH, where the processing slider decides how wide the tune is. With the KEYBOARD switch on as well, the keys transpose the whole pattern.

steps.title: A pluck on Gate 1
steps.why:
The envelope into LEVEL 1, transient and short, so each trigger is a struck note.
- Cord: envelope 3 → LEVEL 1, processing 10.
- Envelope transient: attack 10, sustain 9, decay 6.5.
- waveshape 3, TIMBRE 3.

steps.title: The pulser as the clock
steps.why:
Set the pulser to self so it restarts itself, and set the envelope and sequencer to follow it.
- Pulser trigger self, mode trans, PERIOD 6.4 (about a sixth of a second).
- Envelope trigger source pulser.
- Sequencer trigger source pulser.
- Listen for: a steady stream of plucks on one note.

steps.title: The sequence on PITCH
steps.why:
A blue sequencer jack into PITCH. PITCH processing sets how far apart the stages land: 3.5 spreads the sequencer’s full range over about 14 semitones.
- Cord: sequencer 1 → PITCH.
- PITCH processing 3.5.
- Levels 0, 5, 3, 8.6, 7.2: a five-note tune.
- Listen for: a repeating five-note figure.

steps.title: Rests and reverb
steps.why:
Each stage sends a pulse to the envelope only if its PULSE SEQUENCE switch is up. Set the envelope to fire from the sequencer and switch stage 4 down for a rest.
- Envelope trigger source sequencer.
- PULSE SEQUENCE 4 down.
- REVERBERATION 4.
- Listen for: a gap where the fourth note was.

context.pulser.period: In this sound: the tempo. Up the slider is faster.
context.cosc.pitchCv: In this sound: how wide the tune is. Lower squeezes it into a smaller range; higher stretches it.
context.seq.stages: In this sound: the pattern length. Four or three stages make a different loop from the same sliders.
context.seq.p4: In this sound: down, so stage 4 is a rest. Put it up and the note returns.

tweaks.hear: A shorter, three-note loop.
Slower, about one note every half second.

sounds.name: FM Bell
sounds.ref: Classic technique: audio-rate FM with an envelope on the index
sounds.blurb: The modulation oscillator, at audio rate and following the keys, frequency-modulates the complex oscillator: a struck, glassy bell.
sounds.how: With both oscillators following the keyboard, their ratio stays the same on every key, so every note has the same bell-like colour. The envelope goes to two places: LEVEL 1, to strike the gate, and the modulation input, so the clangy sidebands are strongest at the strike and die away first, the way a real bell’s overtones do.

steps.title: A struck sine
steps.why:
A sine through Gate 1, struck by a transient envelope with a long decay.
- Cord: envelope 3 → LEVEL 1, processing 10.
- waveshape 0, TIMBRE 0.
- Envelope transient: attack 10, sustain 8, decay 3.
- Gate 1 combination.

steps.title: An audio-rate modulator that follows the keys
steps.why:
Switch the modulation oscillator to its high range and its KEYBOARD switch on, and tune it well above the complex oscillator. f.m. osc. mode, index 0 for now.
- range high, KEYBOARD on, waveshape triangle.
- FREQUENCY 3.6: about 1.4 times the complex oscillator’s pitch, a ratio that gives inharmonic, bell-like partials.
- modulation: f.m. osc.

steps.title: The envelope on the index
steps.why:
A second orange jack into the black modulation jack, with its processing slider at 6. The FM is deepest at the strike and fades with the envelope.
- Cord: envelope 1 → modulation input.
- modulation processing 6.
- Listen for: a bright, clangy strike that settles into a purer tone.

context.mosc.freq: In this sound: the ratio between the oscillators, which sets the bell’s colour. Small moves give very different bells.
context.mosc.indexCv: In this sound: how clangy the strike is.
context.env.decay: In this sound: how long the bell rings. Lower on the slider is longer.

tweaks.hear: A different set of partials: more like a gong.
The sound keeps some clang all the way through.

sounds.name: Ring-Modulated Voice
sounds.ref: From the Easel manual — AM up to full ring modulation
sounds.blurb: The modulation oscillator in AM at full index: the complex oscillator ring-modulated into a hollow, metallic tone.
sounds.how: In a.m. osc. mode the modulation oscillator multiplies the complex oscillator. At low index it is a tremolo; at 1.0 the fundamental disappears and only the sum and difference frequencies are left, which is ring modulation. With the modulator following the keys, the metallic colour stays the same up the keyboard.

steps.title: A note on Gate 1
steps.why:
The envelope into LEVEL 1, sustained.
- Cord: envelope 3 → LEVEL 1, processing 10.
- waveshape 2, TIMBRE 1.

steps.title: Slow AM first
steps.why:
In a.m. osc. mode with the low range, the modulation oscillator is a tremolo.
- modulation: a.m. osc., index 4.
- range low, FREQUENCY 6 (5 Hz), triangle.
- Listen for: the note pulsing in volume.

steps.title: Up to audio rate and full index
steps.why:
Switch to the high range, follow the keys, and take the index to 10. The tremolo becomes too fast to hear as a pulse and turns into new frequencies.
- range high, KEYBOARD on, FREQUENCY 5.2.
- index 10: full ring modulation.
- Listen for: a hollow, robotic, bell-like tone with no clear fundamental.

context.mosc.index: In this sound: at 10 only the sidebands are left. Below 5 the original note returns underneath.
context.mosc.freq: In this sound: the ratio that sets the metallic colour.
context.mosc.wave: In this sound: triangle for a smoother ring; square or sawtooth adds many more sidebands.

tweaks.try: Set the modulation oscillator to square
tweaks.hear: A much harsher, buzzier ring.

tweaks.try: Switch the modulation oscillator’s KEYBOARD off
tweaks.hear: Each note now has a different, clashing colour.

sounds.name: Random Pitch, Timbre and Level
sounds.ref: From the Easel manual — Patch-chart 16
sounds.blurb: The self-running pulser calls up a new random pitch, timbre and loudness on every cycle.
sounds.how: Three of the four white random jacks go to PITCH, TIMBRE and LEVEL 1. The pulser, running on its own, triggers the random source, so every period brings a new combination. The processing sliders decide how wide each random range is. Nothing is played: the Easel improvises.

steps.title: The pulser triggers the random source
steps.why:
Set the pulser to self and the random source’s trigger to pulser.
- Pulser trigger self, mode trans, PERIOD 6.8.
- Random trigger source pulser.

steps.title: Random pitch and timbre
steps.why:
Random 1 into PITCH and random 2 into TIMBRE. With the KEYBOARD switch off the pitch comes only from the sliders and the random voltage.
- Cords: random 1 → PITCH, random 2 → TIMBRE.
- PITCH processing 5 (about 20 semitones of spread), TIMBRE processing 7.
- KEYBOARD off.

steps.title: Random loudness
steps.why:
Random 3 into LEVEL 1, so each new note has its own loudness and brightness; some are almost silent.
- Cord: random 3 → LEVEL 1, processing 9.
- Gate 1 combination.
- REVERBERATION 5.
- Listen for: an endless, chattering stream of notes, each one different.

context.pulser.period: In this sound: how often a new note arrives.
context.cosc.pitchCv: In this sound: how wide the random melody ranges. Low values give small, close steps.
context.cosc.timbreCv: In this sound: how much the brightness varies from note to note.

tweaks.hear: A murmur of nearly the same note, varying in tone and loudness.
A fast, bubbling stream of random notes.

sounds.name: Gates in Series: Echoes
sounds.ref: From the Easel manual — Figure 16, simulated echo with changing timbre
sounds.blurb: Gate 1 shapes each note, and Gate 2, struck over and over by the pulser, chops it into echoes, each with a different tone.
sounds.how: With the gate 2 source switch at series, Gate 1’s output feeds Gate 2, and with channel A down only Gate 2 is heard, so both gates must be open for sound. Gate 1 opens with the envelope on each touch and dies away slowly; the pulser’s falling ramp strikes Gate 2 again and again, turning the long note into repeats. The pulser also steps the sequencer, whose voltage on TIMBRE gives each repeat its own colour.

steps.title: Gate 1: a long fading note
steps.why:
The envelope into LEVEL 1, transient with a long decay.
- Cord: envelope 3 → LEVEL 1, processing 10.
- Envelope transient: attack 10, sustain 8, decay 1.5.
- waveshape 1, TIMBRE 2.

steps.title: Gate 2 after Gate 1, struck by the pulser
steps.why:
Gate 2 source at series, channel A down and channel B up. The pulser’s ramp into LEVEL 2 strikes Gate 2 on every cycle.
- gate 2 source: series.
- channel A 0, channel B 10.
- Cord: pulser 1 → LEVEL 2, processing 10. Gate 2 combination.
- Pulser trigger self, mode trans, PERIOD 6.2.
- Listen for: each note broken into fading repeats.

steps.title: A different tone on each echo
steps.why:
The pulser steps the sequencer, and a blue sequencer jack goes to TIMBRE, so each repeat has its own brightness.
- Sequencer trigger source pulser; levels 10, 8, 5, 3, 0.5.
- Cord: sequencer 2 → TIMBRE, processing 8.
- REVERBERATION 4.

context.pulser.period: In this sound: the time between echoes.
context.env.decay: In this sound: how many echoes you hear before the note has gone.
context.out.a: In this sound: at 0, so only the chopped sound of Gate 2 is heard. Bring it up and the plain note comes back underneath; the gates are out of phase, so they also partly cancel.

tweaks.hear: The plain note returns under the echoes, thinned where the two gates cancel.
Fast repeats, like a flutter.

sounds.name: Noise Surf
sounds.ref: Classic technique: the preamp’s noise through Gate 2
sounds.blurb: The Easel’s noise source, through Gate 2 as a lowpass filter, opened and closed by a slow modulation oscillator: waves on a beach.
sounds.how: With nothing plugged into the aux jack, the preamp hears the Easel’s own noise. Setting the gate 2 source to the preamp sends that noise to Gate 2. A slow triangle from the modulation oscillator’s green jack sweeps Gate 2’s LEVEL, and in lo pass filter mode that sweeps the brightness of the noise, rising and falling like surf.

steps.title: Noise into Gate 2
steps.why:
Gate 2 source to the centre position, the preamp, which hears noise when nothing is plugged into aux in.
- gate 2 source: preamp.
- channel A 0, channel B 8.
- Gate 2 lo pass filter, LEVEL 5.
- Listen for: a steady, muffled hiss.

steps.title: A slow sweep
steps.why:
The green mod out jack carries the modulation oscillator as a voltage. Into LEVEL 2 it sweeps the filter.
- Cord: mod out → LEVEL 2, processing 6.
- range low, FREQUENCY 1 (about 0.6 Hz), triangle.
- Gate 2 LEVEL 3.5.
- REVERBERATION 5.
- Listen for: the hiss swelling and falling back every couple of seconds.

context.mosc.freq: In this sound: how often a wave arrives.
context.lpg2.level: In this sound: the brightness at the bottom of each wave.
context.preamp.gain: In this sound: high makes the noise rougher and louder.

tweaks.try: Set the modulation oscillator to sawtooth
tweaks.hear: Each wave rises slowly and drops away at once.

tweaks.try: Switch the preamp gain to high
tweaks.hear: Rougher, louder surf.

sounds.name: Arpeggiated Plucks
sounds.ref: In the style of Kaitlyn Aurelia Smith
sounds.blurb: Held chords broken into bright, rippling lowpass-gate plucks by the 218e’s arpeggiator.
sounds.how: The 218e’s arpeggiator plays the held keys one after another, and each step is a new touch, so the envelope strikes Gate 1 for every note. A little FM from a slow modulation oscillator keeps the tone moving. Hold a chord and let it run.

steps.title: A pluck on Gate 1
steps.why:
The envelope into LEVEL 1, transient and short.
- Cord: envelope 3 → LEVEL 1, processing 10.
- Envelope transient: attack 10, sustain 9, decay 6.
- waveshape 3 with the triangle, TIMBRE 4.

steps.title: Arpeggiator on
steps.why:
Set the pattern to ascending and the rate to about eight notes a second.
- ARPEGGIATION PATTERN: ascending.
- RATE 6.
- Listen for: the held chord broken into a rising ripple.

steps.title: A slow wobble and some space
steps.why:
A little FM from a slow modulation oscillator, and reverb.
- modulation f.m. osc., index 1; range low, FREQUENCY 3.
- REVERBERATION 5.

context.kbd.arpRate: In this sound: the speed of the ripple.
context.cosc.timbre: In this sound: the brightness of each pluck.
context.kbd.arp: In this sound: ascending. Random scatters the same notes.

tweaks.hear: The same notes in a scattered, shifting order.
Longer notes that overlap into a shimmer.

sounds.name: Vactrol Marimba
sounds.ref: Classic technique: a struck bar from a sine and a lowpass gate
sounds.blurb: A sine struck through Gate 1, with the 218e’s velocity adding harmonics to the harder notes, like a mallet on a wooden bar.
sounds.how: A short envelope strikes Gate 1 in combination mode, and the vactrol’s slow fall gives each note a woody ring that darkens as it dies. A little TIMBRE folds the sine into a rounder bar tone. The green vel. jack, how hard the last key was struck, goes to TIMBRE, so loud notes are brighter as well as louder, as with a real mallet.

steps.title: A sine with a touch of folding
steps.why:
Turn the waveshape knob fully left for the sine and add a little TIMBRE.
- waveshape 0.
- TIMBRE 1.5: the sine starts to fold, which adds a few soft upper harmonics.
- Listen for: nothing yet; the gate is still shut.

steps.title: Strike the gate
steps.why:
The envelope into LEVEL 1, transient, with a fast attack and a decay of about half a second.
- Cord: envelope 3 → LEVEL 1, processing 10, LEVEL offset 0.
- Envelope trigger source keyboard, mode transient; attack 10, sustain 9.5, decay 5.
- Gate 1 combination.
- Listen for: a round, wooden note that dulls as it fades.

steps.title: Velocity into TIMBRE
steps.why:
The green vel. jack on the 218e carries how hard the last key was struck. Into the TIMBRE jack it folds the sine further on the harder notes.
- Cord: vel. → TIMBRE, TIMBRE processing 4.
- REVERBERATION 2.
- Listen for: the accented notes of the riff coming out brighter and more knocking than the soft ones.

context.cosc.timbre: In this sound: the colour of a soft note. Up for a harder, more metallic bar; 0 for a plain sine.
context.cosc.timbreCv: In this sound: how much brighter a hard note is than a soft one. At 0 every note has the same colour.
context.env.decay: In this sound: the length of the ring. Lower on the slider gives a longer bar, like a vibraphone without its motor.
context.lpg1.mode: In this sound: combination, so each note loses its top as it fades.

tweaks.try: Push TIMBRE processing to 9 and play some notes hard and some soft
tweaks.hear: Hard notes turn into a clanging metal bar; soft ones stay wooden.
Each bar rings for a couple of seconds and the notes overlap.

sounds.name: Blooming Gong
sounds.ref: Classic technique: FM with an inverted envelope on the index
sounds.blurb: A low FM strike whose clangy overtones grow as the note fades instead of dying first, the way a large gong blooms after it is hit.
sounds.how: The modulation oscillator, at audio rate but not following the keys, frequency-modulates the complex oscillator, so each note gets its own set of inharmonic partials. The envelope strikes Gate 1, and a copy of it goes through the INVERTER into the modulation input: while the envelope is high the index is low, and as it falls the index rises. So the note starts fairly plain and turns more metallic as it rings out. The inverter is what makes this possible on the Easel without a second envelope.

steps.title: A long, low strike
steps.why:
A sine through Gate 1, struck by a transient envelope with a decay of several seconds.
- Cord: envelope 3 → LEVEL 1, processing 10.
- waveshape 0, TIMBRE 1.
- Envelope transient: attack 10, sustain 8, decay 0.8.
- Gate 1 combination.
- Listen for: a deep, plain note that rings for a long time.

steps.title: A fixed audio-rate modulator
steps.why:
Switch the modulation oscillator to its high range with its KEYBOARD switch off, so it stays on one frequency while the keys move the complex oscillator. The ratio between them then changes from key to key, which gives every note different, inharmonic partials.
- range high, KEYBOARD off, waveshape triangle.
- FREQUENCY 3.3.
- modulation: f.m. osc., index 1.5.
- Listen for: a slightly rough, clangy edge on the note.

steps.title: The envelope, turned upside down, on the index
steps.why:
Patch a second orange jack into the INVERTER’s input and its blue output into the black modulation jack. The inverter gives 10 minus the envelope, so the modulation is lightest at the strike and deepest as the note dies.
- Cords: envelope 1 → INVERTER input; INVERTER output → modulation input.
- modulation processing 5.
- REVERBERATION 5.
- Listen for: the overtones swelling and churning a second or two after each strike.

context.mosc.indexCv: In this sound: how far the gong blooms. At 0 the note stays as plain as at the strike; at 10 it ends in a roar of partials.
context.mosc.index: In this sound: the clang at the moment of the strike, before the inverted envelope adds to it.
context.mosc.freq: In this sound: the modulator’s fixed frequency. Small moves change the whole set of partials.
context.mosc.kbd: In this sound: off, so each key gives a different ratio and a different gong.
context.env.decay: In this sound: how long the gong rings, and so how long the bloom takes.

tweaks.hear: A much wilder tail: the note breaks up into noise-like clang as it fades.

tweaks.try: Switch the modulation oscillator’s KEYBOARD on
tweaks.hear: Every note now has the same colour: more of a tuned bell than a gong.

sounds.name: Folded Glide Lead
sounds.ref: Classic technique: a wavefolded triangle with a new colour on every touch
sounds.blurb: A folded triangle lead that glides between notes, with the random source picking a new brightness each time you touch a key.
sounds.how: The waveshape knob turned fully right takes the triangle, which TIMBRE folds back on itself into a reedy, buzzing tone. A white random jack goes to TIMBRE, and the random source is triggered from the keyboard, so every note gets a different amount of folding: some soft, some snarling. PORTAMENTO SLOPE on the 218e makes the pitch slide from note to note, and a slow modulation oscillator adds a light vibrato.

steps.title: A sustained triangle on Gate 1
steps.why:
The envelope into LEVEL 1, sustained, so the note holds while the key is held.
- Cord: envelope 3 → LEVEL 1, processing 10.
- Envelope sustained: attack 8.5, decay 6.
- waveshape 10 with the switch on triangle, TIMBRE 3.
- Gate 1 combination.
- Listen for: a hollow, slightly reedy tone.

steps.title: A random brightness on each touch
steps.why:
Random 2 into TIMBRE, with the random source triggered by the keyboard.
- Cord: random 2 → TIMBRE, TIMBRE processing 6.
- Random trigger source keyboard.
- Listen for: each note of the riff with its own colour, from soft to buzzing.

steps.title: Glide and vibrato
steps.why:
Turn up PORTAMENTO SLOPE so the pitch slides between notes, and give the modulation oscillator a slow, shallow FM.
- PORTAMENTO SLOPE 6.
- modulation f.m. osc., index 1; range low, FREQUENCY 6 (about 5 Hz), triangle.
- REVERBERATION 3.
- Listen for: notes that bend into each other, with a gentle waver.

context.cosc.timbre: In this sound: the least folding any note gets. Raise it for a harder lead overall.
context.cosc.timbreCv: In this sound: how far apart the random colours are. At 2 the notes differ only a little; at 10 some are pure and some are harsh.
context.kbd.porta: In this sound: how long the slide between notes takes. 0 for clean jumps.
context.mosc.index: In this sound: the depth of the vibrato. At 2 it becomes a wide wobble.

tweaks.hear: Some notes nearly pure, others growling: the riff turns unpredictable.

tweaks.try: Set the random trigger source to pulser, with the pulser on self
tweaks.hear: The colour now changes in the middle of held notes, on the pulser’s clock.

sounds.name: Sequence with Chance
sounds.ref: In the style of Charles Cohen’s Music Easel improvisations
sounds.blurb: The pulser runs the sequencer, the sequencer plays the tune through the keyboard pitch input, and the random source colours every note differently.
sounds.how: The pulser, set to self, clocks the sequencer. A blue sequencer jack goes into the black keyboard pitch input, which the complex oscillator follows in semitones exactly as it follows the keys: a full voltage is 28 semitones, so each level slider is a note. The sequencer also triggers the random source, whose voltages go to TIMBRE and to the modulation input, so the same five notes come round with a different brightness and clang each time. A stage switched off leaves a rest.

steps.title: A pluck fired by the sequencer
steps.why:
The envelope into LEVEL 1, transient and short, fired by the sequencer’s pulses.
- Cord: envelope 3 → LEVEL 1, processing 10.
- Envelope trigger source sequencer, transient: attack 10, sustain 9, decay 6.
- waveshape 2, TIMBRE 1. Gate 1 combination.

steps.title: The pulser clocks the sequencer
steps.why:
Pulser on self, sequencer stepped by the pulser.
- Pulser trigger self, mode trans, PERIOD 6.3.
- Sequencer trigger source pulser, STAGES 5.
- Listen for: a steady run of plucks on one note.

steps.title: The sequence plays the keyboard input
steps.why:
Patch a blue sequencer jack into the black pitch jack under KEYBOARD INPUTS. It replaces the 218e’s key voltage, so the complex oscillator, whose KEYBOARD switch is on, plays the sequencer in semitones. One step of the level slider is 2.8 semitones.

sounds.name: Breathing Drone
sounds.ref: Classic technique: a self-cycling envelope and the inverter on two gates
sounds.blurb: The envelope in self mode swells and fades the complex oscillator by itself, while the inverter brings the modulation oscillator up a fifth in the gaps.
sounds.how: In self mode the envelope starts again each time it finishes, so it cycles without anyone touching a key. It opens Gate 1 and adds TIMBRE, so each swell grows brighter as it gets louder. A copy of the envelope goes through the INVERTER to Gate 2, which carries the modulation oscillator tuned a fifth above: as one voice breathes in, the other breathes out. Hold one key to choose the note.

sounds.name: Pressure Voice

sounds.how: The 218e gives a pressure voltage on the violet jacks. Here one goes to LEVEL 1 and another to TIMBRE, so the gate opens and the tone brightens together with the pressure. In this app pressure comes from how hard you strike a key and holds while the key is down, so play some notes hard and some soft: on the hardware you would press harder or lighter into the touch plate as the note sounds. When you let go, the gate closes on its own slow fall.

sounds.name: Tremolo into Ring
sounds.ref: Classic technique: a keyboard-tracking AM oscillator crossing into audio rate
sounds.blurb: Low notes pulse with a tremolo; as the line glides up the keyboard the tremolo speeds up until it turns into a growling ring modulation.
sounds.how: The modulation oscillator is in its low range, in a.m. osc. mode, with its KEYBOARD switch on. It follows the keys in semitones just as the complex oscillator does, so every octave up doubles its rate. At the bottom of the keyboard that is a slow tremolo; three octaves up it is fast enough to be heard as new frequencies, which is ring modulation. Portamento lets you hear the change happen in one slide.

sounds.name: One-Patch Drum Kit
sounds.ref: Classic technique: drums and a shaker from one self-running patch
sounds.blurb: Gate 1 plays kick and toms from the sequencer, Gate 2 shakes noise on every pulse, all clocked by the pulser.
sounds.how: The pulser is the clock. Its falling ramp, from the yellow jack, strikes Gate 2, which carries the preamp’s noise, so every pulse is a short shaker hit. The pulser also steps the sequencer, whose voltage goes into the keyboard pitch input to give each drum stage its own pitch and into TIMBRE to give it its own colour. The sequencer’s pulses fire the envelope, which strikes Gate 1, and a PULSE SEQUENCE switch turned down leaves a stage for the shaker alone.

sounds.name: Seven from Three Stages
sounds.ref: Classic technique: the sequencer setting the pulser’s period
sounds.blurb: A three-stage sequence sets the length of each beat, long-short-short, for a limping seven-eighths pulse that you play notes over.
sounds.how: A blue sequencer jack goes to the pulser’s PERIOD input, so the stage the sequencer is on sets how long the next beat lasts. With three stages, a low first level gives one long beat and two higher levels two short ones, in the ratio three to two: 3 + 2 + 2, seven eighths. The other blue jack goes through the INVERTER to TIMBRE, so the long beat, the lowest voltage, is the brightest: the accent falls on the one. The keys still choose the note.

sounds.name: Two Voices in the Spring
sounds.ref: In the style of Kaitlyn Aurelia Smith’s slower Easel pieces
sounds.blurb: Both oscillators, a fifth apart, swell slowly through both gates and slide between notes into a full spring reverberation.

The Easel is monophonic, so the pad is made from one note and its fifth, not chords.

sounds.name: Silver Apples Pulse
sounds.ref: In the style of Morton Subotnick — “Silver Apples of the Moon” (1967)
sounds.blurb: A bubbling five-note pattern that plays itself, each note a soft, round ping, with one stage left silent and the tone brightening on the higher notes.
sounds.how: This is the patch Subotnick built his early Buchla records on: the pulser runs as a clock, the five-stage sequencer steps on each pulse, and its blue jacks play the tune on PITCH while the same voltage folds the tone on TIMBRE, so the high notes are also the bright ones. The envelope is fired by the sequencer, not the keyboard, so a stage whose PULSE SEQUENCE switch is down plays no note at all: that is the rest in the pattern. The keyboard only transposes it.

sounds.name: Five Against Six
sounds.ref: In the style of Caterina Barbieri — “Ecstatic Computation” (2019)
sounds.blurb: A fast, even arpeggio through a six-note chord whose tone shifts in a five-step pattern, so the accents keep sliding against the notes.
sounds.how: The 218’s arpeggiator plays the six held keys from the bottom up, one at a time. Every new arpeggio note is a fresh touch, so it also steps the sequencer, which is set to the keyboard as its trigger. The sequencer drives TIMBRE in a five-stage pattern of folding, so a six-note cycle of pitches meets a five-note cycle of tones: the pattern only comes round again after thirty notes, the slow-shifting phase music Barbieri builds from a few voltages.

sounds.blurb: Warm, rounded keys with a soft edge on each note and a slow, seasick pitch wobble, like a worn tape of a jazz record.
sounds.how: The tone is a sine folded a little through TIMBRE, a warm, rounded keys sound, and the envelope adds more folding at the start of every note for a soft attack edge. The wobble is the modulation oscillator in its low range, below one cycle a second, frequency-modulating the pitch by a fraction of a semitone: the wow of a stretched tape, made by the oscillator meant for vibrato.

sounds.name: Vibraphone Tremolo
sounds.ref: In the style of Satoshi Ashikawa — “Still Way (Wave Notation 2)” (1982)
sounds.blurb: Soft, ringing vibraphone notes that pulse with a gentle tremolo as they fade, placed sparsely in a calm room.
sounds.how: A vibraphone gets its shimmer from fans turning in the resonators, a tremolo of loudness. Here the modulation oscillator, in its low range at five cycles a second, is set to a.m. osc. at a shallow depth, so it pulses the complex oscillator’s loudness; it does that before the gate, so the tremolo rides on every note as it fades. The envelope is transient with a long decay, a struck bar ringing on.

sounds.name: Felt Piano Keys
sounds.ref: In the style of C418 — “Minecraft – Volume Alpha” (2011)
sounds.blurb: Soft, muted piano-like notes, gently struck ones dark and firmer ones a little brighter, each fading into a quiet tail.

sounds.name: Expanding Universe Arpeggio
sounds.ref: In the style of Laurie Spiegel — “The Expanding Universe” (1980)
sounds.blurb: A slow, even arpeggio through four-note chords whose notes ring for different lengths, some clipped, some ringing on, in a pattern that keeps shifting.
sounds.how: The arpeggiator plays the held chord one note at a time, and every arpeggio note is a fresh touch, so it also steps the sequencer, which is set to the keyboard. The sequencer’s voltage goes to the envelope’s decay input, so each of its five stages sets the length of one note: a five-step pattern of long and short against four-note chords, so the long notes land somewhere new each time round, slowly unfolding like Spiegel’s process pieces.

sounds.name: Shakuhachi Breath
sounds.ref: In the style of Goro Yamaguchi — “A Bell Ringing in the Empty Sky” (1968)
sounds.blurb: A breathy bamboo flute: each note starts with a rush of air and scoops up into tune from just below, then hangs in a quiet room.
sounds.how: The pulser is not a clock here but a second envelope: set to the keyboard and to transient, it fires one falling ramp at each touch. One yellow jack sends that ramp to LEVEL 2, where Gate 2 carries the Easel’s noise, so every note begins with a burst of breath that thins away, the muraiki of the shakuhachi. Another sends it to PITCH with the polarity switched to −, so the note starts a little flat and rises into tune as the ramp falls, the player’s meri scoop. The tone itself is a nearly pure sine faded in slowly through Gate 1.

sounds.name: Open and Closed Hats
sounds.ref: In the style of Cybotron — “Clear” (1983)
sounds.blurb: Ticking sixteenth hi-hats with an open hat hissing on the off-beats, a clangorous metal under the noise.
sounds.how: The envelope is set to sustained, so it holds Gate 2 open for exactly as long as each key is down and then falls in a few milliseconds: short keys are closed hats, long keys open ones, all from the same patch. The hiss is the preamp’s noise through Gate 2 as a plain amplifier. Under it, Gate 1 carries the metal: a square, fixed at a high pitch, frequency-modulated by a square from the modulation oscillator at an inharmonic ratio, a clangorous chord like the six oscillators of a drum machine’s hats.

sounds.name: Pulser Handclap
sounds.ref: In the style of Hashim — “Al-Naafiysh (The Soul)” (1983)
sounds.blurb: A splattering electro handclap on the backbeat, a quick flurry of noise strikes smeared into one big clap in the room.
sounds.how: A handclap is several hands striking a few milliseconds apart. The pulser makes that: set to the keyboard and sustained, it repeats every 25 ms while a key is held, and the envelope fires from it, so a short touch strikes Gate 2 three times in quick succession. Gate 2 carries the preamp’s noise with its gain high, and the vactrol’s slow fall smears the strikes into a single, splattering clap. A little of a heavily folded tone on Gate 1, struck by the same envelope, is the snap of the palms.

sounds.name: Two-Square Cowbell
sounds.ref: In the style of Tito Puente — mambo cowbell on “Ran Kan Kan” (1949)
sounds.blurb: A clanking cowbell driving a mambo pattern, mouth and heel of the bell on two pitches.

Both Easel oscillators make one each: the complex oscillator’s square through Gate 1, and the modulation oscillator’s square, following the keys a fifth above and not modulating anything, through Gate 2. The same envelope strikes both gates, and in combination each strike darkens quickly into the bell’s dull ring.

sounds.name: Tabla Teentaal
sounds.ref: In the style of Zakir Hussain — tabla in teentaal
sounds.blurb: A tabla playing the sixteen-beat teentaal theka, ringing dayan strokes and booming bayan strokes that swoop as the palm presses the skin.
sounds.how: The dayan’s ring is a sine pinged through Gate 1 with FM at one to one opened by the envelope, so each high stroke has a bright, metallic “na”. sounds.name: Talking Drum Squeeze
sounds.ref: In the style of King Sunny Adé — “Juju Music” (1982)
sounds.blurb: A talking drum chattering through a jùjú phrase, every stroke rising in pitch just after it lands, as if squeezed under the arm.
sounds.how: The pulser, set to the keyboard and transient, fires one ramp at each stroke, falling from 10 to 0 over a third of a second. The INVERTER turns that upside down into a ramp that rises, and patched to PITCH it bends each stroke upward as it rings, the player squeezing the drum’s cords. A slow-ish PORTAMENTO adds slides between strokes, and the drum itself is a sine pinged through Gate 1.

sounds.name: Self-Playing Electro Kit
sounds.ref: In the style of Newcleus — “Jam on It” (1984)
sounds.blurb: A self-running electro beat: a dropping kick and a crackling, folded snare on the backbeat, with a hiss on every eighth.
sounds.how: The pulser is the clock, eighths at 120, and it steps the sequencer through four stages whose PULSE SEQUENCE switches make the pattern: stage 1 a kick, stage 3 a snare, stages 2 and 4 rests. The sequencer’s pulses fire the envelope, which strikes Gate 1 and drops the pitch. A blue jack into the keyboard pitch input tunes each stage, the other into TIMBRE folds the snare stage into a buzzing crack and leaves the kick clean. The pulser’s own ramp, on every eighth, strikes Gate 2’s noise for the hats.

sounds.name: Alpha Chance Bells
sounds.ref: In the style of David Rosenboom — “Brainwave Music” (1974)
sounds.blurb: Soft FM bells that play themselves at uneven moments, each at a pitch between the keys and each ringing for a different time, some a second, some a tick.
sounds.how: Rosenboom let brainwaves choose the notes; here the random voltage source stands in for the brain. The pulser is a clock, and each of its pulses calls up four new random voltages. Random 1 moves the pitch anywhere within an octave, off the equal-tempered grid. Random 2 goes to the envelope’s decay input, which shortens the decay by its voltage, so every bell rings for a different length. Random 3 goes back into the pulser’s own PERIOD, so the next pulse comes sooner or later. The bell itself is FM at four to one, struck brighter by the envelope on the modulation input.

sounds.name: Cistern Resonance
sounds.ref: In the style of Pauline Oliveros — “Deep Listening” (1989), recorded in an underground cistern
sounds.blurb: A reedy, accordion-like drone and a fifth above it, swelling and folding brighter by themselves in a long, cavernous reverberation.
sounds.how: No key is needed: Gate 1 is in lo pass filter mode, which passes the sound at a fixed gain and only opens and closes its filter, and its LEVEL slider holds it a little open, so the triangle drones on its own. The envelope is set to self, so it cycles by itself from the first moment, slowly, and two of its orange jacks open the filter further and fold the triangle brighter, a breathing swell like a bellows. Gate 2 adds the modulation oscillator a fifth above, and the spring reverberation is turned all the way up, the forty-five second echo of the Fort Worden cistern squeezed into a spring.

sounds.name: Crystal Shards
sounds.ref: In the style of Maggi Payne — “Crystal” (1982)
sounds.blurb: High, glassy splinters in a five-step pattern with two rests, each splinter a slightly different clangour of glass.
sounds.how: The pulser clocks the sequencer, and the sequencer fires the envelope, so two stages with their PULSE SEQUENCE switches down are rests. Sequencer 1 sets the pitch, a fifth and a minor seventh above the root. The glass is FM at about three and a half to one, a ratio with no common partials, so the spectrum is inharmonic and brittle; each sequencer pulse also calls up a random voltage on the modulation oscillator’s FREQUENCY input, which nudges the ratio, so no two shards ring quite alike.

sounds.name: Foghorn in the Bay
sounds.ref: In the style of Ingram Marshall — “Fog Tropes” (1981)
sounds.blurb: A low, buzzing foghorn that groans up into its note, holds, and sags down again as it fades across a foggy bay.
sounds.how: A diaphone foghorn starts below its note, sounds, and drops with a grunt as the air runs out. The inverter makes that from the one envelope: envelope 2 goes into the inverter, whose output is ten minus its input, and that goes to PITCH with the polarity at −. At rest the inverter sits at 10, so the pitch is held low; as the envelope rises the inverter falls and the pitch climbs into tune; as the envelope fades the pitch sags again. The tone is half square, half sine, through Gate 1 in combination, in a long spring.

sounds.name: Rainforest Cross-Feedback
sounds.ref: In the style of David Tudor — “Rainforest” (1968)
sounds.blurb: Unstable, chattering electronic squawks that bloom once a second, each a different knot of tangled feedback.
sounds.how: The two oscillators are patched in a loop. The modulation oscillator frequency-modulates the complex oscillator as usual, and a cord takes the complex oscillator’s own audio back into the modulation oscillator’s f.m. in, so each one bends the other: the loop never settles, and small changes tip it into squawks, chirps or growls, the way Tudor’s resonating objects fed back on themselves. Once a second the pulser fires the envelope and calls up a new random voltage on the modulation oscillator’s FREQUENCY input, which throws the loop into a new knot.

sounds.blurb: A little robot babbling while a key is held: quick bleeps and warbling whistles at random pitches and in nervous, uneven bursts.
sounds.how: Burtt built R2-D2 from whistles and synthesiser bleeps. The pulser, started and held on by the keyboard, fires a short envelope again and again, and each pulse calls up new random voltages. Random 1 throws the pitch about by up to an octave and a third, random 2 deepens a fast low-range FM warble by a different amount, and random 3 changes the pulser’s own period, so the chatter rushes and hesitates like speech.

sounds.name: Flying Saucer Warble
sounds.ref: In the style of Tom Dissevelt and Kid Baltan — “Song of the Second Moon” (1957)
sounds.blurb: A pure, high whistle that swells in and wobbles wider and wider as it comes, then glides off to the next note, a 1950s flying saucer.
sounds.how: The saucer is a sine with a slow FM wobble from the modulation oscillator in its low range. The envelope has a slow attack and does two jobs: envelope 3 swells Gate 1, a plain amplifier so the high whistle is not dulled, and envelope 1 goes to the modulation input, so the wobble grows from a shiver into a wide siren as the note swells. A long portamento makes the saucer glide from note to note.

sounds.name: Transporter Shimmer

sounds.name: Ray-Gun Zap
sounds.ref: In the style of the sound effects of late-1970s arcade games such as “Space Invaders” (1978)
sounds.blurb: A buzzy “pew” on every key: the pitch dives two octaves and the sound dies with it in a fifth of a second.
sounds.how: The pulser is not a clock here but a one-shot: set to the keyboard and to transient, it fires one falling ramp at each touch. One yellow jack takes the ramp to PITCH, so the note starts two octaves up and dives, and another takes it to LEVEL 1, so the same ramp is the loudness: the zap and its fade are one gesture. The envelope still has a job: envelope 1 folds the sine half of the tone at each touch for a hot, buzzing start.

sounds.name: Biohazard Lab Alarm
sounds.ref: In the style of Gil Mellé — “The Andromeda Strain” (1971)
sounds.blurb: A buzzing two-tone alarm, a tritone apart, beeping in a cold three-step loop with a gap, in a sealed laboratory.
sounds.how: The sequencer set to three STAGES makes the alarm: two stages a tritone apart on PITCH, and a third whose PULSE SEQUENCE switch is down, so it fires no envelope and is the gap. Each beep is a square switched by a short transient envelope through Gate 1 as a plain amplifier, and the modulation oscillator, at the top of its low range, chops the loudness twenty times a second for an electric buzz.

sounds.name: Sonar Ping
sounds.ref: In the style of the sonar pings in submarine films such as “Run Silent, Run Deep” (1958)
sounds.blurb: A pure, high ping every two seconds that rings out and wavers slightly as it dies into a deep, echoing sea.
sounds.how: The pulser, slow and running by itself, fires the envelope every two seconds. The envelope is set to transient with a short hold and a long decay, and it opens Gate 1 as a plain amplifier, because a high sine in combination mode would be dulled and cut short as the gate’s lowpass closed. A slow, shallow FM makes the long tail waver like a sound through water, and the spring, turned high, is the ocean.

sounds.name: Dripsody Water Drops
sounds.ref: In the style of Hugh Le Caine — “Dripsody” (1955)
sounds.blurb: Round, liquid drops falling at uneven moments, each one a little “bloop” that bends up, at a new pitch every time.
sounds.how: Le Caine built Dripsody from one recorded water drop. On the Easel a drop is a sine whose pitch flicks upward as it sounds: a short envelope fired by the pulser goes to PITCH with the polarity at −, so each drop starts low and bends up as the envelope dies. The pitch of each drop comes from chance: random 1 is patched into the keyboard’s pitch input, which the oscillator’s KEYBOARD switch follows in semitones, so every drop lands on a new note, and random 2 changes the pulser’s period, so the drips fall unevenly.

sounds.name: Cicada Chorus
sounds.ref: In the style of Chris Watson — “Outside the Circle of Fire” (1998)
sounds.blurb: A shrill, buzzing insect chorus that swells up, holds and fades again by itself, with a dry rasp under it, in the heat of the day.
sounds.how: A cicada’s song is a high, ringing click repeated hundreds of times a second. The complex oscillator plays the spike, high up, and the modulation oscillator in its high range ring-modulates it through a.m. osc. with a square, chopping it into a buzzing, metallic pulse. Nobody plays it: the envelope is set to self, so it starts at once and swells the chorus up and down over and over, opening Gate 1 and, through envelope 2, a rasp of noise on Gate 2.

sounds.name: Cavern Heartbeat
sounds.ref: In the style of Lustmord — “Heresy” (1990)
sounds.blurb: A slow, deep lub-dub heartbeat, each thump dropping in pitch, the first beat heavier than the second, booming in a cavern.
sounds.how: The rhythm of a heartbeat is uneven, a short gap and a long one, and the sequencer makes it by setting the pulser’s period. Each beat is a low sine thump, its pitch dropped by the envelope on PITCH, and sequencer 2 on TIMBRE makes the first beat rounder and the second softer.

sounds.name: Shortwave Morse
sounds.ref: In the style of “The Conet Project” (1997), recordings of shortwave numbers stations
sounds.blurb: A thin Morse tone spelling dashes and dots through crackling, fading shortwave static.
sounds.how: The trick is the envelope’s sustain input. The envelope is set to transient, so each tone lasts the time on its sustain slider, and sequencer 1 goes to the sustain input, which shortens that time by its voltage: a stage at 0 leaves a dash, a stage a little higher cuts it to a dot. The pulser steps the sequencer and the sequencer fires the envelope, and stage 4’s PULSE SEQUENCE switch is down, the gap between letters. Gate 2 adds the preamp’s noise as static, with random 1 on its level fading the signal in and out.

sounds.name: Geiger Counter
sounds.ref: In the style of Kraftwerk — the Geiger counter that opens “Radio-Activity” (1975)
sounds.blurb: Dry, random ticks and crackles, sometimes a lone click, sometimes a rattling burst, as the counter finds something.

sounds.name: Dalek Ring-Mod Voice
sounds.ref: In the style of Brian Hodgson — the Dalek voices of “Doctor Who” (1963)
sounds.blurb: A grating, metallic monotone barked out in syllables while a key is held, every syllable a different vowel.
sounds.how: Hodgson made the Daleks by ring-modulating an actor’s voice with a 30 Hz tone. Here the voice is a folded triangle, and the modulation oscillator at the very top of its low range, 33 Hz, multiplies it at full a.m. osc. depth, which is ring modulation: the voice’s own pitch disappears into a harsh, metallic pair of sidebands. The pulser, held on by the key, chops the voice into syllables, and the random source gives each syllable a new vowel on TIMBRE.

sounds.name: Dial-Up Handshake
sounds.ref: In the style of a 1990s dial-up modem connecting
sounds.blurb: A screeching, warbling stream of tones leaping about fourteen times a second over a hiss, the sound of a modem connecting.
sounds.how: A modem’s handshake is a stream of tones changing faster than the ear can follow, with a scrambled hiss. The pulser ticks fourteen times a second and each tick puts a new random voltage on PITCH, so the tone leaps about at random. The same ticks step a three-stage sequencer into the modulation oscillator’s FREQUENCY input, so the FM ratio cycles in threes and the tone keeps changing colour, warbling and screeching. Gate 2 adds a steady wash of the preamp’s noise.

sounds.name: Series Phase Swirl
sounds.ref: In the style of Tonto’s Expanding Head Band — “Zero Time” (1971)
sounds.blurb: A bright, hollow chord tone with a slow, swirling phase sweep through it, like a jet passing through the sound.
sounds.how: The two gates are 180 degrees apart: each turns its signal upside down. With Gate 2 set to series, it hears Gate 1’s output, and with both channels in the mix the two partly cancel. Where Gate 2’s lowpass lets the sound through, the lows cancel and a hollow, thin tone is left; move its cutoff and the cancelling sweeps through the spectrum like a phaser. The modulation oscillator, very slow, does the moving from its mod out jack into LEVEL 2.

sounds.name: Kosmische Ratio Drift
sounds.ref: In the style of Ash Ra Tempel — “Schwingungen” (1972)
sounds.blurb: A low drone whose overtones bloom into a new chord every second, unison, fifth, octave, fourth, all smeared in a spring pushed hard.
sounds.how: The drone sounds with no key: Gate 1 is in lo pass filter mode, held open by its LEVEL slider. The sequencer drives the modulation oscillator’s FREQUENCY input, so the FM ratio steps through four settings, unison, a fifth, an octave and a fourth above, and each one makes a different chord of overtones from the same low note. Each step also fires the envelope, which raises the FM depth and opens the filter a little more, so every new ratio blooms and settles. The spring is pushed nearly all the way, so the changes wash into each other.
